title: The more he cut
hookLine: a Sikh saying of those days: the persecutor was a sickle, the Sikhs a crop that grew back

lines: MOW IT, AND IT COMES BACK.
cards: Mow a lawn on Saturday, and by the next weekend it's back. Cut a pot of mint down to stubs, and it pushes out new leaves. Gardeners know this about some plants: cutting doesn't finish them.
Now carry that into Punjab in the hard years, when the governor at Lahore was hunting Sikhs.
Out of those years comes a short saying, passed from mouth to mouth, that turns the whole terrible situation into a picture from the fields.

teach.b: Here's the saying in plain English, since it's a Punjabi folk verse and loses its rhyme in translation. Mannu is our sickle.

teach.h: WE ARE THE CROP HE CUTS.
teach.b: We are the crop he cuts.

teach.h: THE MORE HE CUTS, THE MORE WE GROW.
teach.b: And the more Mannu cuts us, the more we grow. Take it in pieces. First, the sickle: a curved, handheld farm tool, used at harvest by people who have cut wheat all their lives.
The saying takes a feared governor and turns him into a tool in a field. Not a dragon. Not a demon.
A sickle. That alone is a kind of courage, and a kind of humor, the dark humor people find when things are at their worst. Second, the crop.
The Sikhs picture themselves as something growing, rooted in the soil of Punjab, not as soldiers or victims. A crop belongs to the land. Third, the turn.
The more he cuts, the more we grow: the gardener's knowledge from the hook, said in defiance. Cutting doesn't finish what has roots.
Sikh tradition says the community did keep coming back through those years; that's the story this path has been following, from the hiding to Sirhind. Fourth, the plant itself.
The Punjabi word in the saying, soe, is often glossed as dill, a kitchen-garden herb, not a field of wheat. Some readers hear it simply as a crop.

teach.h: SOE: A HERB THAT COMES BACK.
teach.b: Either way, the picture is of something small and green that comes back when it's cut, like the mint in the hook.

how: The saying about Mannu's sickle is still repeated in Sikh history talks and Punjabi retellings of the eighteenth century as a picture of the community's resilience.

games.q: you're a Sikh in the hard years. the governor at Lahore is hunting your people. the villagers want words for what they're living through. what do they say?
o: he is a demon who will destroy us all.
he is our sickle, and the more he cuts, the more we grow.
we must hide and say nothing.
games.why: the saying made him a sickle and the Sikhs a crop: cutting doesn't finish what has roots.

practice: Think of something that cut you back recently, a no, a loss, a plan that fell apart, and picture it as a sickle, just a tool that passed through.
Then look for the roots, what's still there after the cut, a friend, a skill, your breath right now, and picture one new leaf on it. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: datri, a sickle. From a Sikh saying of the hard years: Mannu is our sickle, we are his crop, and the more he cuts, the more we grow. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi for datri, a sickle, the tool in the Sikh saying about Mannu.

carryVoice: Your line: we grow back. Roots outlast the sickle, season after season. Day eight hundred seventy-four, done.
